title: The Payback Test Most Dental Practices Skip Before They Sign for New Equipment
excerpt: Every equipment pitch a dental practice sees promises a return. Few principals test the payback maths first, especially once associate commission splits are factored into the number.
content:
A dental equipment rep has almost certainly stood in your practice this year with an intraoral scanner, a CBCT unit or a same day crown mill, and a story about the patients you will win and the referrals you will keep in-house. The clinical case is often genuine. The commercial case is the part that rarely gets tested before the finance agreement is signed.

Most dental principals we speak with can tell you what a new piece of equipment cost. Fewer can tell you how many extra scans, crowns or same day cases it needs to produce each month before the repayment stops being a drag on the practice's margin. That gap between the purchase decision and the payback calculation is where a lot of otherwise profitable practices quietly lose ground.

This is not a case of principals being careless with money. The decision usually gets framed as a clinical one first and a financial one second, if it gets framed as financial at all, and spring conference season is exactly when the pitch is loudest.

The Pitch Versus the Payback

Every equipment pitch is built around the best case: the machine that pays for itself within eighteen months once patients start requesting it by name. What the pitch rarely accounts for is the ramp up period, the training time that comes off the clinical roster while the team learns the new workflow, and the weeks where a new process actually slows chair throughput before it speeds it up.

A cleaner way to test the decision is to work backwards from the finance repayment itself. If the monthly repayment is a known, fixed number, the practice needs a known, fixed increase in production to cover it, checked against realistic patient volume rather than the number in the vendor's case study. That means pulling the practice's own production report for the procedure the equipment is meant to support, not the average across the profession the rep quotes from a conference slide.

What Commission Splits Do to the Maths

In practices running an associate model, the payback calculation is more complicated than it looks, because a share of every additional dollar the equipment generates leaves the practice as commission before the principal ever sees it. A scanner that lifts an associate's production nicely might only lift the practice's net margin by a fraction of that, once the commission split and any lab fees are accounted for.

This is not a flaw in the associate structure, which is simply performing a different function, rewarding clinical output rather than capital decisions. It does mean the equipment decision needs to be modelled at the practice level, not the chair level, before it is signed off. A principal who buys a scanner expecting it to behave like a principal-owned chair is comparing two different economics without realising it.

The Question That Changes the Decision

The question worth asking before any capital purchase is not "will this equipment help the practice" but "what does this repayment compete against for the next three years." A decision made chair by chair, in isolation, rarely produces the same answer as one made against the practice's full set of priorities, whether that is a second associate, a fit out, or simply building the cash reserve. Equipment finance and a second associate's guaranteed base often draw from the same pool of available capacity, and the practice can usually only comfortably fund one of them in a given year.

A Capital Allocation Review exists for exactly this kind of decision, weighing where capital is going against the return it is actually generating before the next piece of equipment gets added to the surgery. Principals across Brisbane dental practices we work with usually find that running this test changes which piece of equipment gets bought first, not whether new equipment gets bought at all.

None of this argues against investing in modern equipment. Patients notice it, associates want to work with it, and a well-run practice usually needs to keep pace with its own market. The difference between a good investment and an expensive one gathering dust in the corner is whether the payback was tested before the purchase order went in, not worked out afterwards from a profit and loss that no longer adds up the way the principal expected.

faqs.q: How long should new dental equipment take to pay for itself?
faqs.a: There is no single benchmark that suits every practice, but a useful test is whether the additional production the equipment generates comfortably covers its finance repayment within the first two to three years, once realistic patient volume is used rather than a best case projection. If the maths only works using the vendor's own numbers, the payback period is probably longer than it looks.

faqs.q: Does an associate's commission structure change how equipment ROI is worked out?
faqs.a: Yes. A share of the extra revenue new equipment generates through an associate's chair leaves the practice as commission before it reaches the bottom line, so the return at the practice level is smaller than the return at the chair level. Modelling the purchase against practice-wide margin, not associate production alone, gives a more honest answer before the finance agreement is signed.

faqs.q: Should a dental practice lease or buy new clinical equipment?
faqs.a: The answer depends on cash position, tax treatment and how quickly the technology is likely to date, more than on which option feels safer. Leasing preserves cash and shifts obsolescence risk away from the practice, while buying can suit equipment with a long useful life and steady demand. Either way, the repayment or lease cost should be tested against realistic production before it is committed to.

faqs.q: How can a dental practice tell if new equipment will actually get used?
faqs.a: Look at the roster before you look at the brochure. Equipment only earns its keep if there are clinical hours booked to run it, which means checking associate and hygienist availability, patient demand for the procedure it enables, and whether existing chair time is already fully utilised. A machine bought ahead of the capacity to run it usually sits idle longer than expected.

faqs.q: Does buying new equipment affect what a dental practice is worth at sale?
faqs.a: It can, in both directions. Modern, well-maintained equipment can support a buyer's confidence in future production, but unpaid finance attached to underused equipment shows up as a liability without a matching lift in earnings, which a buyer will price in immediately. A business valuation will usually flag this gap clearly, well before a sale process starts.

faqs.q: How do practices work out if a big equipment finance repayment is affordable?
faqs.a: The repayment needs to be tested against the practice's existing cash rhythm, not just its average monthly surplus, since dental cash flow moves with patient volume, health fund payment timing and staff leave. Building this into a cash flow forecast before signing avoids discovering the strain only after the first few repayments land.

faqs.q: What financial mistakes do dental practices make when buying new equipment?
faqs.a: The most common mistake is treating the purchase decision as purely clinical and letting the finance repayment become a fixed cost without a matching plan to generate the extra production needed to cover it. A close second is comparing the new equipment only against doing nothing, rather than against the other ways the same capital could have been used across the practice.
